source: Newell, Shaw, Simon (1958) Elements of a theory of human problem solving
finding: Sets the aim: a theory must be a program that actually solves problems, and must explain set and insight. A theory is memories, primitive processes, and rules for combining processes into programs.
numbers: n/a
quote: It should explain how human problem solving takes place: what processes are used, and what mechanisms perform these processes.
limits: Programmatic statement. Human match is argued, not tested statistically.
agent_relevance: Our schema is the same kind of object: explicit processes plus explicit combination rules, run by code.

source: Newell, Shaw, Simon (1958) Elements of a theory of human problem solving
finding: Logic Theorist (LT) proved theorems of Principia Mathematica by selective search, with three methods tried in order: substitution, detachment, chaining. Detachment and chaining make new subproblems that go on a list and get the same treatment.
numbers: First 52 theorems of Chapter 2, axioms stored, theorems stored as proved: LT proved 38 (73%). About half took under 1 min each; most others 1 to 5 min; a few 15 to 45 min.
limits: One program run on one theorem set. No human data in this paper for the same sequence; the authors say a naive human would be needed per sequence.
agent_relevance: Early version of our S3-S5 loop with subgoals. Proof time rose sharply, maybe exponentially, with proof length, so long chains need decomposition.

source: Newell, Shaw, Simon (1958) Elements of a theory of human problem solving
finding: Selectivity, not speed, explains LT. The brute-force alternative the authors designed would need hundreds or thousands of years for what LT does in minutes. LT tries substitution on only about 10% of stored theorems, chosen by a similarity description.
numbers: Brute-force estimate: hundreds to thousands of years vs minutes. Similarity filter: substitution attempted in about 10% of theorems.
quote: LT's success does not depend on the 'brute force' use of a computer's speed, but on the use of heuristic processes
limits: Brute-force figure is an estimate by the authors, not a run.
agent_relevance: Supports G12: narrow before you search. A cheap similarity filter cut the candidate set about 10 times.

source: Newell, Shaw, Simon (1958) Elements of a theory of human problem solving
finding: Order effects. LT's success on a theorem depends on which theorems it has already stored, like a human's set depends on earlier problems. The same theorem took far longer with all prior theorems stored than with few.
numbers: Theorem 2.48: about 45 min (all prior theorems stored) vs about 15 min (axioms plus Theorem 2.16). A preparatory computation cost about 20 s and saved about one third of time.
limits: Single theorem example. Shows more stored knowledge can slow search (more blind alleys).
agent_relevance: More context is not always better: extra retrieved material widened the search. Matches G11 and G12 on distractors.

source: Newell, Shaw, Simon (1958) Elements of a theory of human problem solving
finding: Insight is redefined as mechanism: either sudden solution after hidden (vicarious) trial and error, or heuristics that keep trial and error small. The authors say absence of overt trial and error does not prove grasp of structure.
numbers: n/a
limits: A definition, not an experiment. Later critics (Ohlsson, Kaplan and Simon) say it leaves out restructuring.
agent_relevance: Insight is not magic. Treat an apparent leap as a search that happened off the page; check by running, not by reading the reasoning (G10).

source: Newell, Shaw, Simon (1958) Elements of a theory of human problem solving
finding: LT's trial and error runs inside a space of possible solutions. Approaching a problem 'meaningfully' means having a strategy that restricts search to a subspace or orders candidates so likely ones come first.
numbers: n/a
limits: Concept paper.
agent_relevance: Names the two levers our operators use: restrict the space, or order the candidates.

source: Newell (1966) On the analysis of human problem solving protocols
finding: Defines the method behind the 1972 book. Subject thinks aloud on a logic task; protocol is split into phrases; a Problem Behavior Graph (PBG) is drawn over a problem space; a production system is fitted to the regularities, with a conflict-resolution rule.
numbers: Cryptarithmetic PBG in this paper has 238 nodes. A second PBG covers about 17 min of one subject (a position analysis). The protocol segment shown is about 12% of the full protocol (last phrase B321).
limits: Single-subject, hours of analysis per minute of behavior. Newell says the actual space the subject uses is unknown and must be conjectured, then tested. Validating the program against the protocol is the open problem.
agent_relevance: A PBG is a log of states and operators. Our own run logs can be analysed the same way to find where an attempt branched and where it stalled.

source: Newell (1966) On the analysis of human problem solving protocols
finding: Formal definition of a problem space: elements are states of knowledge; operators turn one element into another; initial and goal states are both elements. Problem solving is always search from the initial to the goal state.
numbers: n/a
quote: Problem solving takes place in a problem space.
limits: Newell says the theory 'says little' about how a space is selected or built, and that the question is critical.
agent_relevance: This is the S2 REPRESENT gap in our schema: choosing the space matters and is the weakest part of the theory.

source: Newell (1966) On the analysis of human problem solving protocols
finding: Search in a problem space is constructive: states exist only once the solver generates or remembers them. Two paths reaching an equal state give two separate objects unless the solver stores and compares them. So the space is an exponentially growing tree unless memory merges duplicates.
numbers: n/a
limits: Conceptual argument.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side state cache: hash states and drop repeats. The model cannot be trusted to notice it returned to a state.

source: Newell (1966) On the analysis of human problem solving protocols
finding: A solver can hold more than one space at once. Example: a geometry program used a space of symbolic theorems and a space of coordinates; the coordinate space gave much of its power by measuring angles to check assertions.
numbers: n/a
limits: Program example, not human data.
agent_relevance: Matches G3: a second representation (numbers, a diagram, code) gives a check the first space cannot give.

source: Newell and Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search (Turing lecture)
finding: A problem statement is a test plus a generator. To solve a problem is to generate a symbol structure that passes the test. A problem exists when we know the test but the generator does not directly produce a passing structure.
numbers: n/a
quote: To state a problem is to designate (1) a test for a class of symbol structures ... and (2) a generator of symbol structures
limits: General claim, argued by examples (algebra, chess).
agent_relevance: The generate-and-test spine of S3/S4. Having a test is what makes a problem tractable; no test, no safe search (G3).

source: Newell and Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search (Turing lecture)
finding: Search needs information in the space. If solutions are spread at random, no solver beats another. Intelligence needs a pattern that exists, can be detected, and can steer the generator. The amount of search is not a measure of intelligence.
numbers: Tree size is B to the power D (branching B, depth D). The algebra example has B = 1.
limits: Qualitative. Notes the formal theory of heuristic search is thin (a few theorems on alpha-beta, shortest path, best-first).
agent_relevance: Do not search where no signal exists (G12). Cheap signals (checks, differences) are the information.

source: Newell and Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search (Turing lecture)
finding: Two routes against exponential blow-up: build selectivity into the generator, and use differences between current and goal state to steer (means-ends analysis). Selectivity only lowers branching; it does not remove the explosion.
numbers: Best-first rudiments in LT (1955). GPS with means-ends analysis about 1957, with modified depth-first search. Strong chess players seldom explore trees of more than 100 branches; programs explore a million or more.
limits: The chess figure is cited from earlier work, not re-measured here.
agent_relevance: Humans win by sparse branching with good move generation, not depth. Spend budget on proposal quality, not tree size.

source: Newell and Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search (Turing lecture)
finding: Weak methods (best-first, means-ends, hill climbing) are used when knowledge of the space is thin. The authors say brute force is a less promising route, citing modest results of search management in chess.
numbers: n/a
quote: Intelligence for a system with limited processing resources consists in making wise choices of what to do next.
limits: 1976 view. Later hardware and learned evaluators (AlphaGo style) changed the brute-force picture.
agent_relevance: Weak methods are our fallback in S6 IMPASSE; strong task-specific operators come from the problem class lookup in S0.

source: Newell and Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search (Turing lecture)
finding: Problem-space synthesis is unsolved: a symbol system can hold a space and move generators, but how it builds a fitting one for a new situation is 'very much on the frontier'.
numbers: n/a
limits: Still true for LLM agents: the space is chosen by prompt or by the model, with no standard method.
agent_relevance: Reason to treat S2 REPRESENT as a measured step (compare two framings by check outcome), not an assumed one.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar cognitive architecture
finding: Soar runs a decision cycle: input, elaboration (proposal and evaluation), operator selection, application, output. Knowledge is rules that propose, compare and apply operators. When knowledge cannot choose or apply an operator, an impasse creates a substate where the same cycle runs again.
numbers: Three impasse types: state no-change, operator tie/conflict, operator no-change. Real-time behavior needs a decision cycle of about 50 ms.
limits: Description of version 9.6, not an experiment. Soar is mostly tested on hand-built agents.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S6: impasse type decides the response (no operator, tie, cannot apply). Our impasse detector could use these three classes.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar cognitive architecture
finding: Impasse-driven substates give an automatic switch from fast rule knowledge to slower reflective reasoning. Chunking turns the work done in a substate into a rule so the same impasse does not recur. Deliberate reasoning in a substate costs time and can be capped, with a random or non-optimal choice if time runs out.
numbers: n/a
quote: chunking is a learning mechanism that converts deliberate, sequential reasoning into parallel rule firings.
limits: Chunking is learning; our design forbids training. A per-class cache of solved subproblems is the nearest scaffold analogue.
agent_relevance: Doubt only on a signal (G1) is the Soar rule. A cache of resolved impasses is a no-training chunk.

source: Fansher, Shah, Helie (preprint) The effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: Tower of Hanoi, 4-disk then 5-disk, 15-min limit, internal (mental) vs external (computer) presentation. External support raised completion; internal presentation gave fewer moves and longer time between moves.
numbers: Exp 1 (undergraduates): 4-disk completion 100% computer vs 91% mental, chi-square(1)=4.45, p=.03. Time between moves 14.04 s mental vs 7.58 s computer, p<.001. Exp 2 (Prolific, preregistered replication): 4-disk 95.5% vs 87.6%, p=.009; 5-disk 87.4% computer vs 55.3% mental, p<.001.
limits: Modern test of the representation effect, not a replication of Simon and Hayes. Mental condition had a static paper picture. Sample sizes are in the paper's methods; not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Where the state is kept outside the head, the same problem is easier. For an LLM: keep state in code or a scratch file, not only in text.

source: Fansher, Shah, Helie (preprint) The effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: Transfer finding: solving the first problem mentally led to better completion of the harder 5-disk problem, whatever mode was used second.
numbers: Exp 2: 5-disk completion 79.3% after a mental 4-disk problem vs 65.4% after a computer 4-disk problem, B=.98, p=.0488.
limits: Borderline p-value, one experiment; suggestive only.
agent_relevance: Weak hint that forcing explicit planning on a small case helps transfer. Not enough to add a rule (G7).

source: Fansher, Shah, Helie (preprint) The effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: Review passage: a Tower of Hanoi isomorph, Monsters and Globes (Hayes and Simon 1977), has identical structure but people who learn an abstract strategy often fail to transfer to isomorphs. External displays turn a hard memory task into an easy perceptual one (Kotovsky et al. 1985).
numbers: n/a (citing, not reporting)
limits: Secondary report of Kotovsky, Hayes and Simon 1985 and Hayes and Simon 1977; the primary papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: The surface story changes the space the solver builds, so the same logic problem in different words is a different search.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: Casts LLM reasoning as search over thoughts: generate candidate thoughts, evaluate states with the model, search with BFS or DFS and prune. On Game of 24 with GPT-4, plain and chain-of-thought prompting fail; tree search with breadth 5 succeeds on most tasks.
numbers: Game of 24 (100 tasks): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Best of 100 CoT samples 49%; best of 100 IO 33%. About 60% of CoT samples failed already at the first step.
quote: while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%
limits: Task has a crisp check and shallow depth (3 steps). GPT-4 only in the main table.
agent_relevance: The gain appears where an early step can make the problem impossible and a check exists. Lines up with G12 (foothold plus check).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: Mini crosswords (5x5): DFS with model-judged pruning and backtracking beat IO and CoT. Pruning is imperfect and backtracking is essential. Creative writing: ToT passages rated more coherent.
numbers: Crosswords: IO/CoT word-level success under 16%; ToT 60% and 4 of 20 games solved; oracle best state 7 of 20; without backtracking 20% word level. Creative writing coherence (GPT-4 score): IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56; humans preferred ToT over CoT in 41 of 100 pairs, CoT over ToT in 21, 38 equal.
limits: Crossword pruning sometimes cut real solutions (the model judged valid words impossible). Writing score is a model judging model output (see G5, G8).
agent_relevance: Model-judged pruning loses real solutions; keep pruned branches as fallback and use code checks where possible.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: Cost and model dependence. ToT used about as many tokens as 100 CoT trials but won. Weaker models gain less, and generation is the bottleneck, not evaluation.
numbers: Game of 24: ToT 5.5k generated tokens, $0.74 per case, 74%; CoT best of 100 6.7k tokens, $0.47, 49%; IO best of 100 $0.13, 33%. GPT-3.5 ToT 19%. GPT-4 generate plus GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%; GPT-3.5 generate plus GPT-4 evaluate 31%. Creative writing ToT costs about 5x IO/CoT.
limits: Prices are 2023. The best-of-k baselines are oracle choices that real use cannot make without a check.
agent_relevance: Spend the strong model on proposing, a cheaper one on judging. Search costs 5 to 100 times plain, so G7 applies.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: Uses the same LLM as world model (predict next state after an action) and as agent, with Monte Carlo tree search and a reward made of action likelihood, state confidence and self-evaluation. Large gains on Blocksworld planning with LLaMA-33B.
numbers: Blocksworld 2/4/6-step success: CoT 0.17/0.02/0.00; CoT pass@10 0.23/0.07/0.00; CoT with GPT-4 0.50/0.63/0.40; RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42. Average 64% for RAP, a 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT. Test sizes 30/57/114 cases.
limits: Blocksworld has precise, simulator-like structure; LLaMA-33B is weak at baseline. Search budget 10 to 20 iterations per problem.
agent_relevance: Making the state explicit, then searching, rescued a model whose plain run was near zero. Supports explicit S2 state plus search for planning classes.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: On math and logic, gains are smaller. Reward design matters and differs by task. With Llama-2 70B on the full Blocksworld (602 cases), RAP stays ahead on hard (6+ step) cases where CoT collapses.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, Least-to-Most 42.5, RAP(1) 48.6, RAP(10) 51.6. PrOntoQA: RAP prediction 94.2%, proof accuracy 78.8%, 14 points over CoT. Llama-2 hard Blocksworld: CoT 0.22/0.14/0.02/0.02/0.00 vs RAP(10) 0.67/0.76/0.74/0.48 (first columns).
limits: On GSM8K the gap over self-consistency is a few points (51.6 vs 46.8). Action-likelihood reward is key for plans but little help for math.
agent_relevance: Do not expect search to beat plain voting by much on short-chain math (matches G11, G12).

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language agent tree search unifies reasoning, acting, and planning in language models (LATS)
finding: MCTS over agent trajectories with external environment feedback, an LM value function and self-reflection on failed branches. Best scores of its time on HotPotQA, HumanEval and WebShop with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
numbers: HotPotQA exact match, GPT-3.5 reasoning-only: base 0.32, CoT 0.34, CoT-SC 0.38, ToT 0.55, RAP 0.60, LATS(CoT) 0.62. HumanEval Pass@1: GPT-4 base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7; GPT-3.5 ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. Game of 24 GPT-3.5: Reflexion 0.12, ToT 0.20, RAP 0.40, LATS(CoT) 0.44.
limits: Needs an environment that can be reset to earlier states. Authors state higher compute than simple prompting. The coding gain relies on test feedback.
agent_relevance: The gain comes mostly from real feedback (tests, retrieval) inside the search, which is G2 and G3 in practice.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language agent tree search unifies reasoning, acting, and planning in language models (LATS)
finding: Ablations and cost. Removing the LM value heuristic or reflection hurts; DFS is worse than MCTS. Cost grows with samples; LATS expands fewer nodes than ToT and RAP at the same trajectory count.
numbers: HotPotQA EM ablation (ReAct, k=50): ToT 0.39, RAP 0.54, LATS without LM heuristic 0.37, LATS DFS 0.42, no reflection 0.58, full LATS 0.63. Table by k: k=10 ToT 0.34, RAP 0.44, LATS 0.44; k=50 ToT 0.49, RAP 0.54, LATS 0.61. Mean nodes at k=50: ToT 84.05, RAP 66.65.
limits: At small k LATS ties RAP. Numbers are the authors' own, not reproduced here.
agent_relevance: Reflection on a failed branch plus a value signal both count. Keep failed-branch notes as input to S5 only when tied to real failing output.

source: Long (2023) Large language model guided tree-of-thought
finding: An independent ToT design: a controller with a rule-based checker, a memory of states and backtracking around the LLM, tested on Sudoku. Solves more than few-shot CoT as grids grow.
numbers: Ten puzzles per size. 3x3: ToT solved all 10. 4x4: 9 of 10, 80% above one-shot and few-shot. 5x5: 8 of 10, 60% above. One-shot and few-shot fell to about 0.5 on larger grids; zero-shot worst. Round cap 100.
limits: Tiny samples (10 per size). Rule-based controller; ToT misses came from it not seeing dead ends. Not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A code controller with a rule checker and state memory is our design. The failures came from a missing dead-end test.

source: Tian et al. (2024) Toward self-improvement of LLMs via imagination, searching, and criticizing (AlphaLLM)
finding: MCTS with three critics (value, process reward, outcome reward) over option-level steps. Search at decoding time lifts the model, and the search outputs also train it.
numbers: GSM8K with Llama-2-70B: greedy 57.8; AlphaLLM greedy 73.7; AlphaLLM with MCTS 88.9, then 92.0 after more self-improvement (GPT-4 92.0 in the same table). MATH: 20.7 to 23.6 greedy, 48.7 and 51.0 with MCTS. GSM8K ablation: vanilla MCTS 79.5, adaptive branching 84.9, plus PRM 85.9, plus ORM with fast rollout 86.5.
limits: Training is part of the gain, so it is not scaffold-only. Critics are trained on labeled data. Our agent cannot train.
agent_relevance: Shows how much of a search gain is search and how much is training. Decode-time search alone gave about +15 points on GSM8K for a weak base.

source: Newell and Simon (1972) Human problem solving
finding: Not opened (borrow-only scan, full text refused). Known from secondary sources: protocols of subjects on cryptarithmetic, logic and chess are modeled by programs that search a problem space with productions.
numbers: not read
limits: Book claims in this file come from the 1966 precursor and the 1976 lecture, which were read.
agent_relevance: The foundation, but use the opened papers for exact claims.

source: Jeffries, Polson, Razran, Atwood (1977) A process model for missionaries-cannibals and other river-crossing problems
finding: From the catalog abstract only: changing the cover story of four versions did not change the number of legal moves needed but changed the number of illegal moves a lot. A three-stage model with means-ends heuristics, memory assumptions and illegal-move detection fit both.
numbers: not read
limits: Abstract only; full text not accessed.
agent_relevance: Rule violations, not search length, differ with wording. Log illegal proposals separately (G2: check, then revise).

source: Kotovsky, Hayes, Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? Evidence from Tower of Hanoi
finding: Citation only (via Fansher et al. and a vita). Tower of Hanoi isomorphs differ in difficulty, and external displays help. Exact times and the move vs change comparison were not verified from the primary paper.
numbers: not read
limits: Primary paper not accessed. A flashcard summary of Hayes and Simon (1977) gave about 3.5 vs 1.5 minutes to learn change vs move rules; unverified and not used.
agent_relevance: Representation changes cost a lot. Test two framings of the same item before heavy search.

source: Kaplan and Simon (1990) In search of insight
finding: Citation only. Mutilated checkerboard: how the board is labeled changes solving. Search snippets claim 'bread and butter' labels helped most; Bilalic et al. (2019) report chess players did better on it.
numbers: Snippet numbers (1 vs 3.14 hints) unverified and not to be used.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Insight can be treated as search in a second space, the space of representations. Candidate for our reframe step on a signal.

source: Ohlsson (2012) The problems with problem solving: reflections on the rise, current status, and possible future of a cognitive research paradigm
finding: From the abstract only: the enduring contribution of Newell and Simon is that people solve problems by heuristic search in a problem space, but the theory is seriously incomplete. Ohlsson splits the field into five open research questions.
numbers: not read
limits: PDF returned 403; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Confirms where the theory is thin: origin of the space and restructuring.

source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: Newell, Shaw and Simon define a problem as a wish for an outcome you do not immediately know how to reach. They say the theory of problem solving is the study of heuristics: cheap, fallible guides that order, prune or test candidate solutions.
numbers: Report dated 12-30-58, revised 2-9-59; 29 pages; no experimental N in the pages read.
quote: A problem exists whenever a problem solver desires some outcome or state of affairs that he does not immediately know how to attain.
limits: Definition only. Heuristics are said to have empirical, not guaranteed, validity.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G12: search help is used when the answer is not known, and it is not a guarantee. A check must stand behind any heuristic step.

source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: GPS works on objects and operators. Objects have features, and pairs of objects show differences. The program is called general because it separates the problem-solving heuristics from the subject matter: the same core is paired with separate task definitions (logic, trigonometry, algebra, integral calculus).
numbers: Four parts: (1) vocabulary of the task environment, (2) vocabulary of problem-solving organisation, (3) programs defining 2 in terms of 1, (4) task-specific definitions. Items 2 and 3 plus the common nouns are GPS proper.
limits: Generality comes from hand-written task definitions. The authors do not claim GPS learns them.
agent_relevance: Maps to our split between program (generic loop) and slot (task-specific content). Schema section 1 is the same factorisation.

source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: GPS has three goal types: (1) transform object a into b, (2) apply operator q to object a, (3) reduce difference d between a and b. Each goal type has one method. The executive first evaluates a goal (it may reject it as not worth trying), then picks the method, then runs it. Method 1 matches a to b, finds a difference, sets a goal-3 subgoal, then a goal-1 subgoal from the changed object.
numbers: Three goal types, three methods, one executive loop (figures 1 and 2 of the report).
limits: Goal evaluation is only stated, not specified in detail, on the pages read.
agent_relevance: This is the oldest form of S3-S6: generate, test, subgoal on a failing precondition. The 'reject this goal' branch is a budget gate like G12.

source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: All GPS heuristics follow one principle: subgoal reduction, meaning replace a goal by a set of easier goals. This makes GPS highly recursive. The authors add that the principle is only a heuristic: none of the chess or checkers programs then written made essential use of it.
numbers: Statement made in 1958-59 about chess and checkers programs (their refs 1, 3, 6).
quote: Make progress by substituting for the achievement of a goal the achievement of a set of easier goals.
limits: A claim about programs of that date; later chess programs were search-heavy by other means.
agent_relevance: Subgoaling is a design choice for tasks with structure, not a universal gain. Fits G12: use it where there is a foothold.

source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: Means-ends analysis rests on three assumptions: differences between the current and wanted object can be detected; operators change some features and leave others, so they can be indexed by the differences they remove; and some differences are harder to remove than others, so attack the hard difference first even if that adds easier new differences.
numbers: Illustrated with the nursery-school chain: distance, car, battery, repair shop, communication, telephone.
limits: Needs a difference table written per domain. Hard-first ordering needs a ranking of difficulty that the designer supplies.
agent_relevance: For S2 REPRESENT: a usable representation names the differences and the operators that remove each. If the model cannot name the differences, means-ends is not available (see G3: test on the difference, not on fit).

source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: GPS grew out of the Logic Theorist. The Logic Theorist's heuristics came from its designers' introspection. Then the group collected thinking-aloud protocols from college sophomores solving symbolic-logic problems, and built GPS to describe those subjects as closely as possible.
numbers: Subject pool described only as college sophomores; N not given in the report. The fit to subjects is said to be reported in a separate paper.
limits: Fit to human data is deferred to another paper; this report gives design, not a test.
agent_relevance: Evidence trail: heuristics first from introspection, then constrained by protocols. G10 warns that verbal reports are not reliable causes; the later field kept protocols only as data to be coded, never as proof.

source: Newell and Simon (1956) The Logic Theory Machine (RAND P-868, pages 28-50 of the report)
finding: The Logic Theorist proves sentential-calculus theorems with three methods: substitution, detachment, chaining (forward and backward). Detachment and chaining each create a subsidiary problem. Only the substitution method is applied to the subsidiary problem.
numbers: Examples given for theorems 2.01, 2.04, 2.06, 2.08 of Principia Mathematica chapter 2. Detachment: to prove A, find B->A, then prove B. Chaining: to prove a->b, find a->c, then prove c->b.
limits: The pages read do not include the results table. The often-cited count of proofs found out of 52 theorems is covered in the earlier line a02 from the 1958 paper, not here.
agent_relevance: Shows a minimal generate-and-test loop with one level of subgoal, the same shape as S3 to S5 with a cap on depth.

source: Newell and Simon (1956) The Logic Theory Machine (RAND P-868, pages 28-50 of the report)
finding: Search control in the Logic Theorist: failed subproblems go on a list P; the executive takes the simplest one (fewest levels K); it drops duplicates of problems already tried (list Q); it stops when P is empty or when a work tally exceeds a limit, and then reports no proof.
numbers: Work is counted as the number of substitution attempts (tally W). Two stop rules. Priority is smallest number of levels.
quote: it is doubtful whether the program would prove any but the first few theorems of Chapter 2 in a reasonable number of steps
limits: The work measure is one convenient index chosen by the authors, not a validated cost model.
agent_relevance: Direct pattern for our controller: a hard step budget (G12), a duplicate check on repeated attempts, simplest-first ordering, and a rule that failure returns 'no proof' rather than a guess. G6 says we still submit the best attempt, so the stop rule must hand back a fallback.

source: Newell and Simon (1956) The Logic Theory Machine (RAND P-868, pages 28-50 of the report)
finding: Learning in the Logic Theorist is only storage: each proved theorem is saved and becomes a building block. The authors say that without this form of learning the program would stall after the first few theorems.
numbers: Examples: 2.06 proved with the help of 2.05 and 2.04; 2.08 with 2.07.
limits: The program itself does not change; only its theorem memory grows. No count of how much the memory helped is in the pages read (see a04 for the 1958 figures).
agent_relevance: Supports keeping a verified-results store across attempts. It must hold only items that passed a check (G3), or errors will be built upon.

source: Simon (1972) The theory of problem solving (IFIP 71 closing session paper)
finding: Simon defines problem solving as finding the mapping from state descriptions to process descriptions: a path in a graph from the start to a goal. Games need AND/OR graphs because a winning move must work against every reply.
numbers: No empirical N; theoretical review at IFIP 71.
limits: Theory paper by a founder; the generality claim is argued, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Fixes the vocabulary for S2: state description, operators, a goal test, and for adversarial tasks an AND/OR structure.

source: Simon (1972) The theory of problem solving (IFIP 71 closing session paper)
finding: Search size is exponential in depth, and the measure of a heuristic's power is the ratio of the sizes of the searched graph and the full one. For regular graphs with branching b and b' and length L the ratio is (b'/b)^L. Chess mate-finding (MATER) cuts branching from about 20 to 2.
numbers: Graph size b^L; a random goal needs on average G/2 paths. With b 20 to 2 and L 6: 64 million branches to 64.
quote: Reducing b from 20 to 2 reduces the size of a regular graph of length 6 from 64 million branches to 64 branches
limits: MATER pays a price: it fails on checkmates that are not reachable by checking moves. Selectivity is bought with lost completeness.
agent_relevance: Quantifies why G12 matters: a cut in branching is worth far more than a cut in depth cost. Pruning rules must be checked for the cases they lose.

source: Simon (1972) The theory of problem solving (IFIP 71 closing session paper)
finding: Planning in an abstract space shrinks search. If a path of length L is cut into k segments by waypoints, search falls from b^L to k times b^(L/k). Simon also notes that schemes that try promising branches first multiply search by an arithmetic constant, not geometrically, even when s sterile branches are generated beside b productive ones.
numbers: Formula as stated by Simon: k * b^(L/k) versus b^L; extra cost of order (b+s)/b.
limits: The saving needs good waypoints; the paper says abstraction can mean searching for information rather than for a solution. The scan of the (b+s)/b passage is garbled, so read that factor as approximate.
agent_relevance: Gives the maths behind a plan-then-fill step in S1 to S3, and why a wrong plan costs only a constant factor if the plan check is cheap.

source: Simon (1972) The theory of problem solving (IFIP 71 closing session paper)
finding: Ill-structuredness is, in Simon's account, not a different kind of problem. It appears whenever a search system works in an information-rich situation where part of the information lies in the environment or in memory and is evoked only by recognising features. He sees no fundamental difference between ill-structuredness and complexity of the task environment.
numbers: Missionaries-and-cannibals style example: the real world allows a ford, a bridge, an airplane, extra actors.
quote: there is no fundamental difference between this sort of ill-structuredness and complexity of a task environment
limits: This is a defence of the theory against the ill-defined-problem critique, argued by the theory's author.
agent_relevance: For problems with no fixed check, treat the missing structure as information to fetch. Add checks as they appear; do not switch to open-ended chat reasoning.

source: Simon (1972) The theory of problem solving (IFIP 71 closing session paper)
finding: Satisficing is introduced for search problems with bounds: stop at a good-enough solution, either one above a norm or the best found after a set amount of effort. Simon also says completeness of a heuristic is orthogonal to its power, and cites Ernst for conditions under which a GPS difference table guarantees success.
numbers: No numbers beyond the definitions.
limits: Simon argues AI systems need not be complete; this was not tested here.
agent_relevance: Matches G6 and G12: a stop rule and a best-so-far return are part of the theory, not a hack.

source: Simon and Newell (1965) Heuristic problem solving by computer
finding: In 1965 Simon and Newell argue that heuristic programs need not be huge if they search the problem space selectively. They claim a chess program of modest size finds deep checkmating combinations as well as people, and that geometry and integration programs pass school examinations.
numbers: No numbers given in the passages read.
limits: Authors' own survey; claims are about 1960s programs and are not measured here.
agent_relevance: Early statement of the claim that selective search, not raw size, gives power. Compare with the later LLM tree-search results in angle B.

source: Laird and Rosenbloom (1992) In pursuit of mind: the research of Allen Newell (AI Magazine 13(4))
finding: In their account, a problem space is the set of states plus the operators; states are generated dynamically as operators apply, so only a small subset is ever built. One task can be attacked in different spaces: DONALD+GERALD=ROBERT is easier if the space includes column carries, candidate sets and parity, with operators that sum columns and prune sets.
numbers: Cryptarithmetic: states are partial letter-digit assignments; operators assign or test consistency. Protocol segment: D=5 given, subject concludes T=0, then tries R=7.
limits: Retrospective by Newell's students; the protocol detail is a short excerpt.
agent_relevance: Strong case for S2: the choice of representation changes the space and so the difficulty. Our REPRESENT state should try a richer space on impasse, not only more samples.

source: Laird and Rosenbloom (1992) In pursuit of mind: the research of Allen Newell (AI Magazine 13(4))
finding: Newell and Simon revived protocol analysis (thinking aloud, then coding). Newell coded protocols himself. Problem behavior graphs showed that operators and the conditions on states could be written per node, and that is how production systems arose (Newell recalled this in 1991).
numbers: Protocol work 1957 to 1972; production systems 1967 to 1972; the book Human Problem Solving 1972.
limits: Retelling from memory of a participant; the book's own N per task (a few subjects each) is not given here.
agent_relevance: Warns that protocol coding is expensive and subject-specific. Do not treat a model's chain of thought as a protocol (G10); only outputs and checks count.

source: Laird and Rosenbloom (1992) In pursuit of mind: the research of Allen Newell (AI Magazine 13(4))
finding: Pure means-ends analysis was not enough. Human logic subjects switched into short bursts of abstract reasoning, then filled in detail. This led to Planning GPS, the first planner with several levels of abstraction (before ABSTRIPS, 1974). Yet no system matched how humans switched back and forth between levels. In cryptarithmetic many control choices were not a function of the difference to the goal but came from separate pieces of knowledge.
numbers: Planning GPS described in Newell and Simon 1972. STRIPS (Fikes and Nilsson 1971) and Ernst and Newell (1969) cited as heirs.
limits: No numbers on how much planning helped in the human data.
agent_relevance: A hard, honest limit on the single-heuristic story: control often comes from task knowledge. Our operators O1-O8 should be selectable on the task and the impasse type, not fixed to one strategy.

source: Laird and Rosenbloom (1992) In pursuit of mind: the research of Allen Newell (AI Magazine 13(4))
finding: Dates: Logic Theorist 1955-56; first GPS flowchart October 1957; GPS first talks 1958; first GPS publications 1960, more in 1961, the detailed model in 1962; problem spaces named 1965; weak methods 1969; chunking 1981; Soar 1982 (impasse-driven subgoals in 1983).
numbers: GPS research 1957-1963; protocol analysis 1957-1972; production systems 1967-1972.
limits: Secondary timeline. The date 'problem spaces 1965' is the authors' label in a figure.
agent_relevance: Useful for citing the order of ideas: heuristic search first, problem space as the named construct only in 1965 to 1972.

source: Laird and Rosenbloom (1992) In pursuit of mind: the research of Allen Newell (AI Magazine 13(4))
finding: Soar came from frustration that productions had no higher-order organisation. It began as SOR (state, operator, result). Automatic impasse-driven subgoals were added in 1983. R1 was re-implemented as R1-Soar and led to a language for building expert systems at Digital.
numbers: Soar built on XAPS2; chunking idea from 1981. R1-Soar reported by Rosenbloom et al. 1985.
limits: Account of origins only; no performance numbers.
agent_relevance: The impasse-then-subgoal rule is the model for our G1 and S6: act only when a signal says the current method cannot proceed.

source: Laird, Newell and Rosenbloom (1987) SOAR: an architecture for general intelligence (read via a chapter summary, not the paper)
finding: Soar states eleven hypotheses, among them: problem spaces organise all goal-directed behaviour; any decision can become a goal; impasses create subgoals automatically; weak methods arise from task knowledge; chunking is the one learning mechanism. Four impasse types: rejection, tie, no-change, conflict. 52 default productions encode search knowledge such as backtracking and not repeating an operator.
numbers: 11 hypotheses; 4 impasse types; 52 default productions; the 8-puzzle is the worked example.
limits: Opened a chapter summary, not the paper. The summary gives no quantitative results. Stated gaps: no deliberate planning, no new task acquisition, no creation of new task representations, no recovery from over-general chunks.
agent_relevance: Impasse types give a ready list for S6: nothing to try, several equal options, no progress, contradiction. Each can map to one operator.

source: Simon (1975) The functional equivalence of problem solving skills (Cognitive Psychology 7; reprint in Models of Thought vol 1)
finding: Simon describes four Tower of Hanoi strategies that all solve any number of disks: goal recursion (needs the idea of moving a pyramid and a stack of goals in short-term memory), a simple perceptual strategy, a sophisticated perceptual strategy, and a move-pattern (rote rule) strategy. The goal-recursion path is of minimal length.
numbers: Minimum moves 2^n - 1. Three disks: seven moves plus three goal-setting steps. In the 4-disk case the simple perceptual rule falls into a non-terminating cycle after the fifth move unless a stack of subgoals is kept.
limits: Analysis of strategies by production systems; a theoretical paper. Fits to subjects are given elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Same task, different internal cost: a scaffold should say which strategy it uses and what memory it needs. A strategy without a goal stack can loop, so add a loop check (G3 on a held-out check, not on the trace).

source: Simon (1975) The functional equivalence of problem solving skills (Cognitive Psychology 7; reprint in Models of Thought vol 1)
finding: The move-pattern strategy is: on odd moves move the smallest disk, on even moves the next-smallest exposed disk, with the smallest disk cycling in a fixed direction chosen by the parity of the number of disks. Only move parity needs short-term memory. It is rote: the reasons for moves are not derivable from the problem definition.
numbers: Needs two stored facts: move parity and cycle direction; cycle direction can sit in long-term memory.
limits: Rote strategies do not transfer by reasoning and break when a rule changes. The scan of the cycle-direction sentence is garbled, so the exact rule for parity is not restated here.
agent_relevance: A learned or cached procedure can be cheap and correct but opaque. Keep checks that detect a cached rule applied outside its range (G3).

source: Simon (1975) The functional equivalence of problem solving skills (Cognitive Psychology 7; reprint in Models of Thought vol 1)
finding: Simon formalises each strategy as a production system with two kinds of productions: general ones and perceptual tests. He assumes that productions place no demand on short-term memory for their own running, and flags this as an empirical assumption on which his STM comparisons depend.
numbers: Production = condition -> action; perceptual tests write features to STM. Strategies compared by STM load and perceptual tests needed.
limits: Stated by Simon as untested at that time.
agent_relevance: Shows how to compare two scaffolds by explicit memory and test demand, not by feel. Useful when we ablate schema elements at equal tokens (G7).

source: Anderson and Douglass (2001) Tower of Hanoi: evidence for the cost of goal retrieval
finding: Anderson and Douglass summarise what followed Simon (1975): participants do not start with goal recursion but often find it (Anzai and Simon 1979 gave a protocol of one participant finding it); time per move rises linearly with the number of new subgoals to create (Anderson, Kushmerick and Lebiere 1993; Ruiz 1987). Not everyone subgoals: one author's child learned the move-pattern strategy from a computer game.
numbers: Anderson et al. 1993 had 28 participants in the 15-step comparison cited in the paper.
limits: Review inside a methods paper; the child example is informal. These earlier studies were not opened.
agent_relevance: Subgoaling cost is real and per-subgoal. Counts as evidence for G11 and G12: each extra subgoal is billed, so spend them only on a signal.

source: Anderson and Douglass (2001) Tower of Hanoi: evidence for the cost of goal retrieval
finding: A redesigned Tower of Hanoi task separates the cost of storing a goal from the cost of retrieving it. Result: retrieval time depends on how long ago the goal was formed; storage time does not depend on how long the goal must be kept. A fitted line gives time = 2.655 + 0.065*Formulate + 0.053*Store + 0.085*Retrieve. An ACT-R model with goal memory like any other memory fits.
numbers: 10 CMU students, 3 days, 21 problems per day, 5 disks, 15-move problems with 7 posted subgoals. Category effect F(2,18)=10.96 (latency); mean latency 2.81 s on day 2 and 2.62 s on day 3; days effect F(2,18)=9.81.
quote: goal memory does not seem different from other memories
limits: Small N (10) and an artificial task where goals are posted by clicking, which makes subgoaling heavier than natural play. Units of the regression assumed seconds.
agent_relevance: Evidence that long goal chains cost accuracy and time through memory retrieval. For a language model, keep the goal stack as program state (schema section 1), not in the prompt text.

source: Anderson and Douglass (2001) Tower of Hanoi: evidence for the cost of goal retrieval
finding: The paper tests the perfect goal stack assumption of Soar and ACT-R and finds it wrong for people: goal storage and retrieval take time and can fail, and participants asked to see the goal stack only 1 to 5 percent of the time in some cells. It concludes a separate perfect stack is not needed.
numbers: Stack inspection requested 5% of the time for action 7 in the Under-5 sequence; 1% in other sequences; 2% in some retrieval cases.
limits: Click-to-see-goals is an indirect measure of forgetting.
agent_relevance: Our program stack is exact; a language model's recall of its own goals is not. This supports keeping goals outside the model.

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: explorations in the problem space of difficulty (Cognitive Psychology 22; CMU archive copy)
finding: The Chinese Ring Puzzle is extremely hard, yet digital versions with the same search space are not. In experiment 1 only 1 of 12 college students solved the real puzzle within 90 minutes, while 25 of 26 solved a digital isomorph. Digital times were 25.48 min (No-Info) and 14.55 min (Lo-Info). Ruger (1910) saw a 4-ring version take 62 minutes on average (median 29, range 2 min to 4 h).
numbers: Exp 1: 26 students; Chinese vs digital F(2,21)=33.72; No-Info vs Chinese t(11)=4.98; Lo-Info vs Chinese t(14)=12.17. Lo-Info solved in 57% of No-Info time (first position).
limits: Community-college students, small cells (12 on the real puzzle); the time cap was used as the time for unsolved cases.
agent_relevance: Same space, very different difficulty: the form of the move operator, not the size of the space, drove it. Test whether our slot prompts make how to make a move clear.

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: explorations in the problem space of difficulty (Cognitive Psychology 22; CMU archive copy)
finding: A move demonstration fixed most of the difficulty of the real puzzle. With a hint, the Chinese puzzle took 79.7 min versus 19.9 (No-Info) and 13.0 (Lo-Info); 24 of 41 still failed in two hours. The hint cut digital times by only 17%.
numbers: Exp 2: 69 students (41 with the Chinese puzzle, 28 with two digital isomorphs); F(2,63)=44.96 for problem type; hint type had no effect, F(1,126)=1.85. Four of the same 41 failed a digital isomorph.
limits: Authors note the 90-minute cutoff in exp 1 may have lowered effort: 17 solvers in exp 2 took under 90 min and 16 of them under 75.
agent_relevance: Showing one worked move may do more than an hour of search. Supports putting one worked example of the operator in the slot, then checking it.

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: explorations in the problem space of difficulty (Cognitive Psychology 22; CMU archive copy)
finding: Search-space size did not set difficulty here. The space is linear (at most two legal moves in a state, one back). Starting 21 or 31 moves from the goal gave no reliable difference in time (F(1,53)=2.12, p<.2). A random walk with a 1-in-5 reversal chance predicts about 242 moves, close to the observed legal moves in the No-Info condition, yet the subjects' move patterns were far from random.
numbers: Exp 4: 42 students (14 new, 28 from exp 2). Short path chosen by 4 of 14 in position one but only 2 of 14 in position two (chi-square 7.145). Anderson's formula M(n)=(n+1)(n-(n-1)p)/p for a chain.
limits: Authors say path choice cannot explain the null; the null result is for linear spaces only.
agent_relevance: Counterexample to a pure bigger-tree-is-harder view. For us: do not assume deeper search fixes a task that is hard because of the move rule.

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: explorations in the problem space of difficulty (Cognitive Psychology 22; CMU archive copy)
finding: Move behaviour was bimodal: long stretches of error-prone, no-progress moves, then a fast error-free run to the goal. Average moves ranged from 150 to 450 for different isomorphs although the minimum was 21. Subjects stalled at barriers (3 reversals in 12 moves) and accelerated after position 15.
numbers: Minimum expected time from move speed: 3.68 s * 21 moves = 77 s, only about 13% of the time actually taken. Subjects tended to judge progress by the number of balls out of boxes; moves from 31 to 21 raise that count 7 times out of 10.
limits: Reading of move records by the authors; the progress heuristic is inferred, not measured.
agent_relevance: Matches impasse and insight pictures: long unproductive search, then a quick finish once the move structure is understood. Our impasse detector (G1) should fire on repeated reversals, not on a timer.

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: explorations in the problem space of difficulty (Cognitive Psychology 22; CMU archive copy)
finding: Showing more information about legal moves helped only when it was easy to use. The All-Info display, with gates and blockers, gave 206 illegal moves per subject without explanation and 46 with it; it was the slowest in first position (about 20.37 min versus 18.92 and 12.29 for the other two). Time per move was much higher in All-Info.
numbers: Exp 3: 42 students. All-Info move time difference significant (F about 17.79, p<.00005).
limits: The assignment of the three times to conditions is read from garbled table text; treat the ordering as probable.
agent_relevance: More context in a prompt is not more help if the model has to decode it. Test every added context block at equal tokens (G7).

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: explorations in the problem space of difficulty (Cognitive Psychology 22; CMU archive copy)
finding: Transfer between isomorphs was weak and partly asymmetric. Between two digital isomorphs, time fell by 47.6% (Lo-Info to No-Info) and 60.5% (No-Info to Lo-Info); in exp 1 only 32% and 31%, not significant. The real puzzle got no transfer from the digital ones.
numbers: Exp 2: F(1,48)=18.03 for transfer, p<.00025. Exp 1 transfer F(1,29)=1.89, p<.2.
limits: Different cell sizes (7 per cell in exp 2 digital pairs). Authors call the explanation tentative.
agent_relevance: Same logic does not guarantee the model transfers a skill across surface forms. Isomorphism checks (G3) should be run on mutated forms, not assumed.

source: Kotovsky and Simon (1990) What makes some problems really hard: explorations in the problem space of difficulty (Cognitive Psychology 22; CMU archive copy)
finding: Kotovsky and Simon recap earlier work: Hayes and Simon (1974, 1977) found Tower of Hanoi isomorphs differing by about 2 to 1 in solution time; Kotovsky, Hayes and Simon (1985) found up to 16 to 1. Most of the time was spent learning to make moves; once moves were fluent, hard and easy isomorphs were solved at about the same speed. They say this challenged the view that the size of the problem space sets difficulty, as did Wason and Johnson-Laird's content effects.
numbers: Difficulty ratio 2:1 (Hayes and Simon) and 16:1 (Kotovsky, Hayes and Simon 1985), measured in solution time; same state space of 27 states.
limits: These two results are quoted from a later paper by the same school, not from the 1974 or 1985 originals, which I could not open.
agent_relevance: Core finding for representation fixes the space: same logical problem, 16 times harder on a worse cover story. Ties to the content-effect documents in A01.

source: Kotovsky and Fallside (1988) Representation and transfer in problem solving (in Klahr and Kotovsky, eds., Complex Information Processing)
finding: Kotovsky and Fallside restate the theory: the external task environment has an objective search space; the problem space is the solver's internal representation, containing the move operators with their legality tests and the knowledge states from start to goal. The isomorph work shows difficulty lives in the internal representation of moves.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi space: 27 states; all but three have three legal moves (back, or two new states); three states with all disks on one peg have two.
limits: A chapter synthesis; claims rest on the 1985 and later experiments.
agent_relevance: Schema S2 should keep the two notions apart: the real task, and the version of it the model holds. We can only test and revise the second.

source: Kotovsky and Fallside (1988) Representation and transfer in problem solving (in Klahr and Kotovsky, eds., Complex Information Processing)
finding: Difficulty of Monster Change versus Monster Move follows how many entities must be imaged to test a move. The hardest isomorph (Monster Change) took about 16 times as long as the easiest (Tower of Hanoi). Tachistoscopic legality judgements were slower when more entities had to be imaged. A Change move needs one more imaged entity than the equivalent Move.
numbers: Difficulty ratio 16:1; Monster Move vs Change about 2:1 (Hayes and Simon). Move rules and planning loads tabulated by entities to image (Table 2).
limits: Summary of 1985 results as given in the chapter, not the original data.
agent_relevance: A concrete model of why a rephrased task is harder: working memory load of the legality test. Hints at a testable property of our prompts: count the items the model must hold to check one step.

source: Kotovsky and Fallside (1988) Representation and transfer in problem solving (in Klahr and Kotovsky, eds., Complex Information Processing)
finding: Two phases in solving: slow exploratory moves that leave the solver as far from the goal as at the start, then a fast final-path run. About two-thirds of subjects with recorded latencies showed long-short and long-short-short latency patterns, read as planning a subgoal-goal pair and then executing. Training on the move operator removed the differences between Monster isomorphs, and final-path times were close to Tower of Hanoi time.
numbers: A 15-move solver with 3 s extra per move would lose 45 s, but the harder problem took 10 to 15 minutes longer. A random-walk simulation used many more moves than subjects even with their bias against backtracking.
limits: Latency patterns are an indirect read of planning; only about two-thirds of subjects fit.
agent_relevance: Practice on the operator, not search, is what shortens solving. In a scaffold: a short warm-up to fix the operator semantics before the real item may beat extra samples. Test it (G7).

source: Kotovsky and Fallside (1988) Representation and transfer in problem solving (in Klahr and Kotovsky, eds., Complex Information Processing)
finding: Transfer depends on move-operator compatibility and is asymmetric when operators differ. Monster Move to Acrobat: +29.5% (hard to easy) against -28.9% (easy to hard), neither significant alone. Monster Move with Reverse Acrobat (compatible operators): +57.4% easy to hard (significant) and +38.5% hard to easy. Predicted difficulty order Peg Move < Dish Move < Dish Change.
numbers: Percent change in solution time as reported; the Peg Move version builds rule 2 into the physical stack so the solver need not remember it.
limits: Small samples; the authors flag significance for only one of the four effects.
agent_relevance: If an external structure enforces a rule (like the stacked disks), the model need not hold it. Put rule enforcement in code, not in the prompt (section 1 of the schema).
